content: AI-Powered Real-Time Market Intelligence for Stocks, Crypto, Forex and Commodities Gap risk is clear for three names heading into Monday. NASDAQ: SPCX closed Thursday at $185.00, down 3.56%, with a Sunday report showing MSCI gave SpaceX its lowest ESG mark. Option markets price in a ±10% swing for the week. NASDAQ: MU soared 8.70% to a record $1,133.99 after Apple flagged higher memory bills. Micron reports earnings Wednesday. NYSE: XOM slipped 2.08% to $137.81 as traders leaned into the de-escalation with Iran, but late Sunday Iran’s Tasnim news agency said Hormuz stays shut pending a Lebanon ceasefire and enforceable oil waivers. U.S. equities didn’t price any of this after Friday’s Juneteenth pause. Monday’s opening auction will take in about 89.5 hours of news and events since Thursday’s 4 p.m. close—24 hours more than a standard weekend. That’s important because the first trade may jump a chart level, skipping over where buyers or sellers might show up. The map here isn’t a prediction; it marks where new demand or forced selling could show up. SpaceX trading setups are complex. Options traders bet on a move between $166–$204 by Friday. CRSP or S&P Dow Jones could add SpaceX to certain indexes as soon as Monday. Underwriting banks will be able to release research after the quiet period ends. But a Financial Times report said MSCI handed SpaceX a CCC ESG rating, which could keep ESG funds away, even if broad index funds look at possible buys. For NASDAQ: SPCX, Thursday’s $172.11–$190.00 zone is the first test. The stock ended the session about 72% up that range, down 3.56% on the day. A move above $190.00 would aim at $201.80, which was Tuesday’s close, then put the $225.64 high back in sight. If it breaks below $172.11, the options market’s floor at $166 could come into play. Micron is seeing momentum traders pile in ahead of a set event. Shares jumped Thursday after Apple announced it would raise prices to cover higher memory and storage costs. According to Reuters, Micron stock was up 298% in 2026 going into its June 24 earnings, with the investor-relations site listing the call for 4:30 p.m. ET Wednesday. Micron’s current fiscal Q3 forecast is $33.5 billion ± $750 million in revenue and $19.15 ± $0.40 non-GAAP EPS. NASDAQ: MU finished Thursday just 1.36% below its record intraday high at $1,149.43, after trading as low as $1,092.79. June 26 options had priced in an expected 14.3% move after the report—about $162 either way from the closing price. That sets up a theoretical range of $971.83–$1,296.15. One side of that move, almost 2.9 times Thursday’s $56.64 intraday range. Exxon is back in focus as a weekend reversal name. The stock dropped on Thursday with traders betting on looser oil flows after word of a U.S.-Iran interim deal. Reuters later tracked 25 commercial ships crossing Hormuz on June 18, the highest since April 18 but way below the pre-conflict average of 120 daily crossings. On Sunday, Tasnim reported that a reopening still depends on a Lebanon ceasefire and U.S. waivers for Iranian oil. That clouds the quick recovery case. NYSE: XOM traded in a narrow range for Thursday, holding between $135.85–$138.46 even with the geopolitical news in play. Shares finished at $137.81, closing about 75% up the range. Volume surged to about 48.1 million shares, around 2.7 times the 50-day average, MarketWatch data showed. June 26 options expiring ahead of the weekend implied a move of ±$4.32 or 3.13%, pegging the market’s expected range at $133.62–$142.26. First resistance is set at $138.46. Micron is 9.5% away from the first upside trigger at $1,149.43, using the explicit information-gain calculation — that’s the distance to the level divided by the option-implied weekly move. Exxon is 15.0% away from clearing $138.46, and SpaceX needs 27.0% to get back to $190.00. These numbers don’t indicate direction. They show MU is mechanically nearest to price discovery. XOM shows the biggest gap between what options price in ahead of the weekend and what a Sunday macro headline could mean. The bear case hangs at three key levels. SpaceX under $172.11 threatens the $166 strike, and a move through there opens up the wider drop to its $135 IPO price. Micron falling through $1,092.79 and then $1,043.19 would wipe out Thursday’s run, with its 298% year-to-date gain giving back plenty of room below. Exxon slipping below $135.85 would cast doubt on the crude closure trade and point to $133.62. Breaks past those marks at the open could trigger stop-loss slips, so the headline chart level won’t always be where trades get filled. First reaction lands when CME oil and U.S. equity-index futures start up again Sunday night. XOM should be the first to show the Hormuz read; SpaceX flows show up in the index and research next; Micron’s main event is still Wednesday’s earnings. Biggest catalyst ahead is whether tanker traffic data backs up Tehran’s closure claim—because a crude move big enough to push XOM outside its 3.13% weekly options band would mean Monday is about repricing physical supply, not just a headline trade. If you are reading the news and thinking the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz ends today’s oil problems, think again. Shipping has started to resume, but normal flows may take weeks or months to recover as markets work through disrupted logistics, damaged infrastructure and depleted inventories. The Iran conflict disrupted a meaningful share of global oil flows, including production, refining and shipping activity. Even with the Strait moving back toward normal operations, oil markets may remain tight through the summer as traders watch weekly storage data and the pace of supply recovery. WTI’s pullback looks encouraging for oil bears, with prices sharply below their 2026 highs as of mid-June. The caveat for oil bears is that the June price drop found support above $75, suggesting the market may not be ready to price in a full return to normal supply conditions. Catalysts will be dwindling storage levels, as reported weekly throughout the summer. Don’t forget, it's summer in the Northern Hemisphere, the most heavily populated half of the Earth and the most active oil-burning period. The takeaway for investors is that energy companies, specifically producers and refiners, are well-positioned. Not only is demand high for their product, but high prices mean high margins. Add in the fact that the sector has invested heavily in efficiency and quality over the past few years, and the odds are high that windfall profits are on the way. Energy-sector earnings estimates have moved sharply higher, but they may still leave room for upside if crude prices rebound and demand remains firm. Estimates, which have more than doubled over the trailing-90-day period, forecast more than 120% earnings per share (EPS) growth in the current quarter and 65% for the year. The likely outcome is that economic strength underpins sector outperformance in Q2, and the upcoming WTI price rebound underpins it in the longer term. ExxonMobil’s dividend is not the highest among energy companies, but it is substantial, yielding nearly 3% as of mid-June. The payout is reliable, having been increased annually for more than 40 years, and the payout ratio remains manageable at around 69% of earnings. Looking ahead, the payout is likely to continue increasing at a modest single-digit rate; buybacks will catalyze share price gains. Unlike most other energy companies, Exxon’s operational quality enabled it to sustain aggressive buybacks despite lower oil prices. The story today is that it can accelerate repurchases, while many of them will need to divert some of the windfall cash flow toward debt payments and reduction. ConocoPhillips' capital return is unique in that it is tied to free cash flow. In this scenario, the company will pay larger dividends and buy back more shares as oil prices rise. The silver lining is that deceleration is already expected, as any downticks in oil prices, margins, and cash flow will also be reflected in the payments. The difference today is that COP is shifting away from a variable payout structure toward more regular payments; these changes in cash flow will be reflected in buyback activity. They are collectively rated as Moderate Buys with a bullish bias and uptrends in their share prices. title: Is ExxonMobil's Guyana Expansion a Game-Changer for XOM Stock - Kavout
content: ExxonMobil (NYSE: XOM) is at a pivotal juncture with its ambitious offshore development plans in Guyana, particularly as it navigates the environmental approval process for the Longtail and Haimara projects. The company's recent submission of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for Longtail and the subsequent public consultations, which began on April 13, 2026, mark a crucial step toward unlocking significant future production. This move is not merely procedural; it represents a strategic doubling down on one of the world's most promising new oil frontiers, potentially reshaping XOM's long-term growth trajectory and shareholder value. However, the path is fraught with environmental and regulatory challenges that demand careful consideration from investors. The proposed Longtail development, ExxonMobil's eighth in the Stabroek Block, is projected to begin production in 2030 and operate for approximately 30 years. This long-term horizon underscores the strategic importance of Guyana to ExxonMobil's portfolio, especially given the project's substantial output estimates of 1.2 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day and around 250,000 barrels per day of condensate. With XOM currently trading at $154.92 as of May 22, 2026, and a market capitalization of $642.14 billion, the successful sanctioning and development of these projects are essential to fuel future earnings growth, particularly against a backdrop of -4.5% year-over-year revenue decline in FY2025. The ongoing public consultations, led by ExxonMobil Guyana President Alistair Routledge, aim to address community concerns and integrate feedback into the EIA process, a critical component for securing final authorization from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The Longtail and Haimara projects are cornerstones of ExxonMobil's aggressive expansion strategy in Guyana's Stabroek Block, a prolific offshore basin that has yielded numerous world-class discoveries. ExxonMobil operates the Stabroek Block with a 45% interest, alongside partners Hess (now owned by Chevron) with 30% and CNOOC with 25%. This consortium has transformed Guyana into a major global oil producer in a remarkably short period, with Longtail representing the eighth and Haimara the expected ninth development within this block. The sheer scale of these developments is staggering; Longtail alone is designed to produce 250,000 barrels per day of condensate and 1.2 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas, contributing significantly to global energy supply for decades. These projects are strategically located in what ExxonMobil Guyana President Alistair Routledge refers to as the "southeast gas area" of the Stabroek Block. Longtail is positioned as the anchor for several discoveries in its vicinity, while Haimara is slated to anchor the subsequent project. The company submitted the Field Development Plan (FDP) for Longtail by the end of March 2026, signaling its readiness to move forward once environmental authorizations are secured. The projected start of production in 2030 for Longtail, with an operational lifespan of roughly 30 years, provides a clear long-term revenue stream for ExxonMobil, bolstering its upstream segment and providing a hedge against potential declines in mature assets elsewhere. For ExxonMobil, these developments are crucial for maintaining its production profile and driving future cash flow, especially as the company navigates a dynamic global energy landscape. The Stabroek Block discoveries have been instrumental in XOM's recent performance, and continued success here is vital for offsetting the -23.1% year-over-year decline in free cash flow observed in FY2025. The consistent stream of new projects, each requiring substantial capital investment but promising high returns, underpins the company's commitment to its fossil fuel portfolio while also acknowledging the increasing demand for natural gas as a transition fuel. The successful execution of Longtail and Haimara will solidify Guyana's role as a core growth engine for ExxonMobil for the foreseeable future. The successful development of the Longtail and Haimara projects in Guyana holds profound implications for ExxonMobil's financial outlook, promising to inject substantial revenue and cash flow into the company's operations starting in 2030. With Longtail alone projected to add 250,000 barrels per day of condensate and 1.2 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas, these volumes represent a significant boost to XOM's overall production capacity. This increased output is critical for a company that saw its revenue decline by -4.5% year-over-year in FY2025 and net income fall by -14.4% during the same period. The new production streams are expected to reverse these trends, providing a much-needed catalyst for top-line and bottom-line growth. From a valuation perspective, ExxonMobil currently trades at a P/E ratio of 25.60, which is relatively high for an integrated oil major, suggesting that investors are already anticipating future growth from projects like those in Guyana. The company's TTM EPS stands at $6.05, and the expected production from Longtail, operating for 30 years, will contribute significantly to future earnings per share. While the immediate impact on financials is still several years away, the certainty of these projects moving forward, contingent on environmental approvals, provides a strong long-term investment thesis. The company's dividend yield of 2.6%, with a payout ratio of 68.1%, is supported by its robust cash generation, which these new projects are designed to enhance further. Moreover, the sheer scale of the Stabroek Block's reserves and the continuous stream of new developments offer a long runway for capital allocation and shareholder returns. The $642.14 billion market cap reflects ExxonMobil's dominant position, but sustained growth requires consistent project execution. The Longtail project's contribution to free cash flow, which saw a -23.1% decline in FY2025, will be vital for improving financial flexibility, funding future exploration, and potentially increasing shareholder distributions. The company's relatively low debt-to-equity ratio of 0.19 and a net debt-to-EBITDA of 0.65 provide ample capacity to finance these large-scale developments, underscoring a disciplined financial approach even as it pursues aggressive growth in Guyana. ExxonMobil's ambitious development plans in Guyana, while promising significant returns, are not without substantial environmental and regulatory hurdles. The Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) process for the Longtail project, which commenced public consultations on April 13, 2026, is a critical phase that requires addressing concerns from local communities and environmental advocates. ExxonMobil Guyana President Alistair Routledge emphasized the importance of these 60-day consultations, stating they are designed to allow residents to review studies and raise concerns, ensuring risks are mitigated. However, past experiences suggest that public engagement in Guyana's EIA process has been limited, with a lack of public awareness and understanding often leading to insufficient feedback, as highlighted in a critical review of the process. A major point of contention revolves around oil spill liability. A June 2023 decision by an appeals court ordered ExxonMobil to put up $2 billion for Guyana oil spill costs, but critically, it shifted the remaining uncapped liability onto the Guyanese people. This decision, which followed a lower court ruling that had initially held ExxonMobil fully responsible, has been widely criticized by organizations like the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) for exposing Guyana to significant financial risk. The 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill, which cost BP and its insurers $70 billion, serves as a stark reminder of the potential scale of such disasters, far exceeding the $2 billion bond. This lack of full financial assurance from ExxonMobil's parent company remains a significant environmental and reputational risk. Furthermore, the legal framework governing oil and gas in Guyana has been described as evolving. The Environmental Protection Act of 1996, initially lacked specific guidelines for the oil and gas sector, which only emerged as a major industry after ExxonMobil's Liza-1 discovery in May 2015. While the EPA now requires EIAs for projects like Longtail, concerns persist about the sufficiency of consultation periods and the adequacy of addressing social and cultural issues. The company's own Oil Spill Response Plan for Guyana Operations, last revised in December 2025, outlines safeguards, but the ongoing debate about liability and transparency, particularly regarding the actual terms and scope of insurance coverage, continues to cast a shadow over ExxonMobil's operations in the region. Guyana has rapidly become an indispensable pillar of ExxonMobil's global strategy, representing one of the most significant growth engines for the energy giant. The Stabroek Block discoveries, initiated with Liza-1 in 2015, have transformed the country into a crucial source of future production, particularly as the company navigates a complex energy transition and seeks to maintain its competitive edge. With an operational interest of 45% in the Stabroek Block, ExxonMobil is heavily invested in unlocking the vast hydrocarbon potential of this region, which is expected to underpin its upstream segment for decades. The Longtail and Haimara projects, slated for production starting in 2030 and operating for 30 years, are central to this long-term vision. The strategic importance of Guyana is amplified by its role in diversifying ExxonMobil's asset base and providing high-margin barrels. Unlike some mature fields that face declining production and higher operating costs, Guyana offers prolific, low-cost production that enhances XOM's overall profitability and resilience. This focus on high-quality, advantaged assets is a core tenet of CEO Darren W. Woods' strategy, aiming to improve capital efficiency and shareholder returns. The projected output of 250,000 barrels per day from Longtail alone, combined with substantial natural gas volumes, will contribute significantly to ExxonMobil's global production targets and cash flow generation, which is crucial given the -5.5% decline in operating cash flow in FY2025. Moreover, Guyana's emergence as a major oil producer reshapes regional energy security and offers a stable, democratic partner for the U.S. in South America. For ExxonMobil, this geopolitical stability, coupled with the sheer scale of the resource, makes Guyana an attractive investment destination despite the environmental scrutiny. The company's commitment to the region is further demonstrated by its ongoing environmental studies and community engagements, aiming to balance resource development with responsible operations. While ExxonMobil has seen its employee count decrease from 61,500 in 2023 to 58,000 in 2025, reflecting broader efficiency drives, the Guyana operations remain a key area of investment and talent deployment, signaling its enduring importance to the company's future. The investment outlook for ExxonMobil (XOM) is intrinsically linked to the successful, and environmentally responsible, development of its Guyana projects. While the Longtail and Haimara developments promise substantial long-term production and cash flow, investors must weigh this against the inherent risks. The company's current P/E ratio of 25.60 suggests that a significant portion of this future growth is already priced into the stock, which closed at $154.92 on May 22, 2026. The market is clearly optimistic about Guyana's potential, but any delays in environmental approvals, increased regulatory burdens, or significant cost overruns could temper this enthusiasm. The ongoing public consultations and the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) requirement for a full Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for Haimara underscore the heightened scrutiny. The $2 billion oil spill liability bond, while substantial, leaves Guyana financially exposed to larger catastrophic events, a risk that could eventually translate into reputational damage or increased regulatory pressure for ExxonMobil. Investors should monitor the progress of these approvals closely, as they represent critical milestones for the 2030 production target for Longtail. Despite a recent -4.5% decline in FY2025 revenue and -14.4% drop in net income, ExxonMobil's strong balance sheet, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.19, provides a solid foundation to absorb the capital expenditures required for these mega-projects. The 2.6% dividend yield remains attractive, supported by the company's long-term cash generation capabilities, which will be significantly bolstered by the 250,000 barrels per day from Longtail. For long-term investors, XOM represents a play on global energy demand and a company with a clear growth pipeline in Guyana, but the narrative will increasingly be shaped by its ability to navigate environmental and social governance challenges effectively. ExxonMobil's strategic focus on Guyana positions it for robust long-term production growth and enhanced shareholder value, provided it successfully navigates the complex environmental and regulatory landscape. The Longtail and Haimara projects are vital for XOM's future, offering a compelling growth story for investors willing to accept the associated execution and environmental risks. (DNTH) jumped 8% on Friday after the company reported positive early data from its ongoing late-stage trial of claseprubart, an experimental drug for chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP). The DNTH stock, on Friday, clocked its best session since early March. CIDP is a rare nerve disorder that causes weakness, numbness and loss of function in the arms and legs. It occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks the nerves. Current treatments often involve frequent infusions or steroids. In the first part of the study, 75% of the initial group of patients showed meaningful improvement after receiving claseprubart, Dianthus said. The company was expecting 50%, and the results clearly exceeded its own targets. The trial has a two-part design. In the initial part, patients received claseprubart. Those who improved were then moved into the next part of the study, where some continued on the drug, and others switched to a placebo. The goal is to see how long it takes for symptoms to return when the drug is stopped. The high response rate in the first part was seen across several measures of how well patients could move and function, the company said. Claseprubart is given as an under-the-skin injection every two weeks using a pre-filled pen, which could make it more convenient than current CIDP treatments like IVIG infusions. Dianthus also said on Friday that it now expects to provide guidance on the timing of the Part B top-line results by the end of 2026. Following the update, investment bank Raymond James reaffirmed its ‘Strong Buy’ rating on Dianthus and kept its price target at $125 per share. The analyst noted that the 75% response rate beat their expectations and stood out favorably compared to Sanofi’s competing drug. They also highlighted that the study’s design — starting with open treatment and then testing what happens when the drug is withdrawn — appears to be a lower-risk approach than the one used in Sanofi’s failed study. Sanofi discontinued its late-stage study of riliprubart in patients with CIDP who had failed or responded inadequately to standard treatments earlier this month. The company announced that an independent data monitoring committee had reviewed interim data and concluded the study was unlikely to meet its efficacy goals. The decision came after riliprubart had shown more modest results in an earlier mid-stage study, where roughly 50% of refractory patients improved at week 24. Sanofi is now evaluating whether to continue its other ongoing late-stage trial in patients already on maintenance IVIg. Microsoft Chief Executive Satya Nadella and Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood have not ruled out a future structural split if it ultimately improves business operations or makes the division easier to sell. Sharma declared that the downward trajectory "cannot continue" amid stagnant global console spending and escalating manufacturing costs. To counter the financial slump, Sharma is executing a dual-pronged strategy of aggressive cost-cutting and targeted blockbusting spending. The Information reported that Sharma is preparing significant layoffs and budget reductions across Xbox’s less-popular game studios. However, those savings will be funneled directly back into the division's most lucrative and recognizable intellectual properties, keeping the overall game development budget relatively flat year over year. Microsoft’s top leadership has tentatively approved an increased game-development budget for the upcoming fiscal year starting in July, specifically targeted at fast-tracking new mainline entries for "industry-defining franchises" that Sharma claims have historically lacked adequate funding. A primary focus of the investment surge includes accelerating development timelines for core franchises like Halo, Fallout, and The Elder Scrolls. The move attempts to address prolonged gaps in major releases; The Elder Scrolls and Fallout have not seen new mainline titles debut since 2011 and 2014, respectively, while the flagship Halo franchise has lacked a major release since 2021. Sharma has informed deputies that the division must publish new Halo games on a significantly faster timeline. As of March 2026, the drug produced meaningful responses in heavily pretreated patients, many of whom had already tried multiple existing therapies, the company said on Thursday. In one key group receiving an 80 mg daily dose, 48% of patients achieved a major molecular response — a standard measure of treatment success in CML — while 30% reached a deeper response. The drug was generally well tolerated, with most side effects being mild. However, 6% of patients discontinued the study due to adverse events, the company noted. The company also announced it has aligned with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on key elements of its planned late-stage trial. Enliven expects to begin the late-stage trial in the second half of 2026. Separately, Enliven priced an upsized public offering to raise capital for its programs. “The gross proceeds from the offering are expected to be around $400.0 million before deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and other offering expenses,” the company said in its pricing announcement. ELVN-001 is now the main focus of Enliven’s pipeline after the company decided last year to explore strategic alternatives for its other clinical program, ELVN-002. title: Prediction: Oil Will Hit $60 a Barrel in 2027. Here's How to Invest Now. - The Motley Fool
content: I think oil will fall back to where it was before the Middle East conflict, but it could be a volatile ride. The one big thing investors have learned from the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East is that oil and natural gas remain vital to the world's normal functioning. This is why most investors should have some exposure to the sector. That said, the next year is likely to be complicated for the energy industry because of the lingering impact of the war. I expect oil prices to fall back to where they were before the conflict in 2027, to around $60 per barrel for Brent Crude. However, getting to that point could be a bit of a rollercoaster ride, as industry fundamentals take center stage as newsflow from the conflict becomes less important. Here's how I'd invest in the energy sector today to prepare. Right now, there is too little oil and natural gas to go around because the Strait of Hormuz has been shut down. The impact of that has been muted by companies and countries working down their oil and natural gas reserves. As the Strait reopens, oil tankers stuck on the wrong side will likely lead to a rush of oil hitting the market, but global reserves still need to be replenished. So oil prices may fall initially, only to rise again as market fundamentals become increasingly important. This is basically what ExxonMobil (XOM 2.08%) and Chevron (CVX 2.36%), two of the world's largest energy companies, have been discussing for months. At this point, the U.S. strategic oil reserve is near levels last seen in 1983. That's a situation that has to be rectified, and it is just one example of what has been taking place around the world. Brent Crude Oil Wholesale Spot Petroleum Price data by YCharts At the same time, there have been fundamental changes in the global energy market. For example, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has left OPEC, freeing it from the production limits set by the group. Also, the United States has ramped up exports, and countries around the world may take an increasing interest in energy security. Then you have to take into account lingering demand changes as countries attempt to reduce energy use to address supply constraints from the conflict. How oil moves will likely be different in the future, and there might actually be more of it, as the International Energy Agency just warned. That would lead to lower energy prices, but only after a period of elevated demand that pushes oil and gas prices higher. The energy sector could be volatile for a bit, and that assumes that the agreement to end the conflict holds. While most investors should probably have some exposure to the energy sector, it is probably best not to attempt to time oil and natural gas prices. Sure, if oil prices rise, companies like Diamondback Energy (FANG 1.07%) and Devon Energy (DVN 1.08%) will likely benefit. It is also appealing that they operate in the onshore U.S. market, far from geopolitical tensions. But when oil prices fall, these producers typically get hit quite hard. A more conservative route is probably better. That's where energy giants like Exxon and Chevron come in. They have assets spread across the world and portfolios spanning the entire energy value chain. This diversification helps to soften the peaks and valleys in the energy market. In addition, they have the two strongest balance sheets in their integrated peer group. They are, basically, designed to survive the entire energy cycle. The strength of these two businesses shines through in their dividends, which have been increased annually for decades. Exxon, the larger of the two companies, has a dividend yield of 2.9% right now. Chevron's yield is 4%. While the most conservative investors may prefer Exxon, the extra yield Chevron offers today probably makes it the more attractive buy for income-focused investors. Either one, however, would be a good option for navigating what is likely to be an unusual year ahead in the energy market. Reuben Gregg Brewer has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. title: Exxon Mobil Shares Slide With Oil, XOM Off 6% for Holiday Week - TechStock²
content: AI-Powered Real-Time Market Intelligence for Stocks, Crypto, Forex and Commodities Exxon Mobil Corp. goes into Monday’s open on the defensive. Shares dropped over the holiday week, with investors cutting the stock as oil’s war premium eased and more crude flowed through the Strait of Hormuz. The stock finished Thursday at $137.81, losing 2.08% on the day after dropping to as low as $135.85 during the session. The New York Stock Exchange did not open Friday for Juneteenth, which meant there was no chance for a regular-session move before the weekend. Crude is back in focus. Brent edged up Friday but looked set for a roughly 8% loss this week after signs of a Lebanon ceasefire and increased movement in Hormuz after the U.S.-Iran peace deal. “The backlog of ships can move quicker than some people think,” Price Futures Group’s Phil Flynn told Reuters. Reuters Exxon gets hit from both sides when oil falls. As an integrated company, Exxon not only drills for oil and gas but also refines, trades and sells fuel. The upstream segment, which covers production and exploration, usually takes the biggest hit when crude drops. On Thursday, Chevron dropped 2.22% and ConocoPhillips slid 3.12%, so the slide went wider than just one stock. Exxon shares moved as traders reacted to the sharp shift in pricing for the marginal barrel, less so to anything on the company’s balance sheet. A geopolitical premium can boost energy stocks in a hurry. It can disappear just as fast. Bank of America, with Jean Ann Salisbury leading the team, has gone bullish on Exxon, TheStreet reported. Analysts upgraded the stock to Buy from Neutral and put a $154 target on it. They said the recent drop already reflects weak long-term Brent and called out Permian performance, refining, and a chance for Middle East volumes to recover. Exxon posted first-quarter earnings of $4.2 billion on May 1, with the company pointing to record production out of Guyana and first LNG at Golden Pass Train 1. CEO Darren Woods said Exxon is built to “perform through disruption and across market cycles.” Bulls may see these results as a sign of strength, but they don’t answer the oil-price drop. Exxon Mobil Corporation Exxon signed a preliminary agreement to supply LNG to Zululand Energy Terminal, which would be South Africa’s first LNG import terminal. LNG is natural gas cooled into liquid for shipping. Andrew Barry, chairman of ExxonMobil LNG Market Development Inc., said the deal “support[s] South Africa’s energy security with reliable supply.” Reuters Rumors on a possible LNG deal stalled. Woodside Energy out of Australia said it was “not aware of any proposal” with Exxon and was not in talks, pushing back on talk that Exxon might target Woodside to boost its LNG and Asia business. Exxon had no comment. Reuters Exxon kept work going on its Guyana pipeline. The company filed for environmental clearance for a 35-well drilling push in the Stabroek block, roughly 120 miles offshore Guyana. The campaign is planned to run from 2028 to 2033. Oil’s outlook remains shaky. If U.S.-Iran talks fall apart or Hormuz faces extra curbs, crude could snap back, taking some pressure off Exxon. But if supplies return quicker and prices slide more, analysts may keep trimming producer earnings forecasts. Oil traders questioned the diplomatic moves and flagged more swings ahead. Exxon (XOM) heads into the week with traders watching the open after four sessions down. The focus is on its South Africa LNG move and the Guyana permit push, both important for the long side. For now, it’s about oil finding its footing and whether XOM keeps above $135-$138. title: Is Exxon Mobil's Recent Surge Sustainable Amid Middle East Tensions - Kavout
content: Exxon Mobil (XOM) stock has been a standout performer in recent weeks, with shares trading at $154.19 as of March 2, 2026, up 1.11% on the day and nearing its 52-week high of $159.35. This impressive run, which saw the stock climb from $115.15 on November 30, 2025, to $152.50 by March 1, 2026—a 32.4% increase—is largely attributed to a dramatic shift in the global energy landscape. The "Midnight Hammer" crisis in the Middle East, characterized by retaliatory strikes and a de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has injected a significant risk premium into crude oil markets. This geopolitical shock has sent oil prices soaring, with WTI crude currently at $71.15 per barrel, having recently spiked towards $73 and Brent crude briefly touching $100 per barrel. The Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for 20% of global seaborne oil, has seen shipping halted and war risk coverage cancelled by marine insurers, effectively stranding an estimated 15 million barrels per day (bpd) of global supply. This immediate supply disruption, combined with a perceived failure of OPEC+ to adequately increase production, has fueled a rapid "risk-off" rotation into hard assets like oil. The market's reaction on March 2, 2026, saw XOM and Occidental Petroleum (OXY) both climb 2.1% by midday, even as the broader S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite tumbled. This divergence underscores a fundamental reassessment of value in an uncertain geopolitical climate, where the "old economy" energy trade has become a defensive hedge. While the immediate catalyst is conflict, the underlying "AI Power Crunch"—the insatiable demand for energy to fuel massive data centers—is also contributing to a structural revaluation of energy companies. However, the sustainability of this surge hinges precariously on the resolution of the Strait of Hormuz standoff. Analysts warn that a diplomatic "off-ramp" within the next 72 hours could lead to a significant cooling of oil prices. Conversely, if the blockade persists, a "super-spike" toward $120 per barrel is possible, which would almost certainly tip the broader global economy into a recession by Q3 2026. This delicate balance means XOM's recent gains, while substantial, are tied to highly unpredictable global events. The current surge in oil prices provides a significant tailwind for Exxon Mobil's Q1 2026 earnings, potentially rewriting near-term cash flow math. Higher crude prices directly enhance the profitability of Exxon's Upstream segment, which saw a 41% increase in revenue in Q1 2025, including a remarkable 234% jump in its U.S. Upstream operations. This segment is particularly sensitive to commodity price fluctuations, making the current environment highly favorable for top-line growth and margin expansion. Despite a 6% decline in net profit and a 15% fall in EPS in Q1 2025 due to weaker refining margins and petrochemicals, the company demonstrated resilience later in the year. Exxon Mobil reported strong Q3 2025 earnings of $7.5 billion and $14.8 billion in cash flow, followed by a Q4 2025 EPS of $1.71, beating estimates. This consistent outperformance, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of earnings beats, suggests an underlying operational strength that can capitalize on improved market conditions. Analysts are already adjusting their expectations, with Bank of America raising ExxonMobil's price target from $135 to $151, reflecting confidence in enhanced future profitability due to the oil risk premium. The consensus Q1 2026 EPS is projected at approximately $1.53, a figure that could prove conservative if oil prices remain elevated throughout the quarter. Exxon's ability to generate substantial free cash flow, projected at $52 billion for the 2025-2026 period, further strengthens its financial position to navigate market dynamics. However, it's not a clear-cut picture. While Upstream benefits, the Energy Products (refining) and Chemical Products segments can face margin pressures. In Q1 2025, Energy Products revenue declined 4% and Chemical Products revenue fell 8%, largely due to falling refining margins and an oversupply in the global chemical market. Therefore, while high crude prices boost one side of the business, investors must monitor product solutions segment margins and overall production guidance during the Q1 2026 earnings call, expected in late April, to gauge the full impact. Beyond the immediate tailwinds from geopolitical tensions, Exxon Mobil's long-term investment thesis is underpinned by its strategic focus on "advantaged barrels" and robust production growth from key assets. The company's operations in Guyana, particularly the Stabroek block, are a cornerstone of this strategy. Projects like Uaru, expected to start up by year-end 2026 with a capacity of 250,000 b/d, and Whiptail, forecast to add another 250,000 b/d next year, are set to boost Guyana's daily oil production well beyond 1 million b/d. Exxon Mobil is also actively developing Guyana's significant recoverable gas resources, especially in the southeast part of the Stabroek block. The Hammerhead project, for instance, is designed to transport gas by pipeline to shore, complementing oil production. The company has already completed its first gas-to-energy pipeline, awaiting an onshore power plant to lower electricity costs in Guyana. This integrated approach to resource development highlights Exxon's commitment to maximizing value from its world-class geology and competitive development costs. The Permian Basin in the U.S. shale patch remains another critical growth engine. CEO Darren Woods has stated there is "no near-term peak Permian" for Exxon, citing over 40 technologies currently in testing to enhance recovery and efficiency. This focus on low-cost, high-margin production in both Guyana and the Permian has made XOM a "HALO" stock (Heavy-Asset, Low Obsolescence) for investors seeking stability and long-term value. Furthermore, Exxon Mobil's commitment to shareholder returns is a significant draw. The company has a strong track record of distributing capital through dividends and share repurchases, having distributed $9.4 billion in Q3 2025 and $9.5 billion in Q4 2025. As a dividend Aristocrat, boasting 26 consecutive annual dividend increases, XOM offers a compelling proposition for income-focused investors, signaling management's confidence in its ability to generate sustained free cash flow and maintain financial discipline. While Exxon Mobil benefits from current market dynamics, several significant risks could derail its long-term investment thesis. The most immediate concern remains commodity price volatility. Despite recent spikes, energy prices are inherently sensitive to geopolitical events, OPEC+ decisions, and global demand fluctuations. A sharp decline in prices, whether due to de-escalation in the Middle East, falling global demand, or oversupply, could significantly reduce ExxonMobil’s income, particularly in its highly profitable Upstream segment. Beyond oil prices, the company faces regulatory and political risks. Stricter environmental legislation globally, including potential bans on exploration in sensitive regions, new emissions standards, and tighter regulation of refining, could increase operating costs or limit production capacity. The accelerating global energy transition to lower-carbon sources poses a fundamental threat to long-term demand for fossil fuels, potentially diminishing Exxon Mobil's core product revenue streams and creating significant market risks. Exxon Mobil's diversified earnings are also susceptible to global chemical market oversupply and weak refining margins. As seen in Q1 2025, the chemical segment experienced substantial earnings reductions due to "bottom-of-cycle" margins. This cyclicality can act as a significant drag, even when other segments perform well. The capital-intensive nature of its upstream and downstream mix constrains revenue growth assumptions, keeping them modest at around 2.3%. Finally, valuation concerns persist among some analysts. With a TTM P/E ratio of 23.15 and a current price of $154.19, some models suggest the stock is trading at a premium. Analyst consensus price targets range around $140-$142, implying a modest downside from current levels. For instance, one model projects a $140.92 fair value, representing a 6% downside. While the company's beta of 0.35 reflects lower volatility than the broader market, a retreat in oil prices after tensions ease could expose valuation risks, making the stock less attractive at current levels. Navigating the current volatile energy market with Exxon Mobil requires a nuanced approach, balancing short-term tactical plays with long-term strategic considerations. For investors looking to capitalize on immediate geopolitical shocks, XOM's strong correlation with oil prices, coupled with its robust production and cash flow, makes it a compelling option. The stock's beta of 0.35 indicates lower volatility compared to the broader market, offering a degree of stability even in turbulent times. However, a purely short-term strategy is fraught with risk. The unpredictable nature of geopolitical events means any sudden de-escalation could lead to a sharp correction in oil prices and, consequently, in XOM's stock. Investors should consider XOM as a "HALO" stock, benefiting from heavy assets and low obsolescence, but remain vigilant. Monitoring key events like OPEC+ ministerial meetings for changes in production quotas, and geopolitical developments in critical regions like Guyana, is paramount. For long-term investors, Exxon Mobil's status as a dividend Aristocrat, with a current dividend yield of 2.6% and 26 consecutive annual increases, offers a compelling income component. This consistent return to shareholders, alongside disciplined capital allocation and share repurchase programs, provides a defensive moat against market fluctuations. The company's strategic investments in low-cost, high-return assets like the Permian and Guyana further solidify its long-term growth potential, irrespective of short-term price swings. To mitigate risks, diversification remains key. While XOM offers exposure to the energy sector, considering alternatives like ConocoPhillips (COP) for a more pure-play upstream focus, or Canadian Natural Resources (CNQ) for its strong inventory and capital discipline, could balance a portfolio. Ultimately, investors should maintain a conservative position sizing, perhaps 1% to 3% of their portfolio, given the stock's near-term volatility and the cyclical headwinds in its downstream and chemical segments. Exxon Mobil stands at a pivotal juncture, poised to benefit from current geopolitical tailwinds while navigating inherent industry volatility. Its strategic asset base and commitment to shareholder returns offer a compelling long-term narrative, but investors must remain acutely aware of the risks.
